posts.title: MacDowell Is Glorious
posts.description: Tell me about a life-changing community or experience for you. I just returned from a glorious five weeks at MacDowell . And I want to share a little of the magic without spoiling the surprises and traditions in store for you. MacDowell is sleepaway camp with particularly brilliant fellow campers. My group was composed of architects, painters, sculptors, poets, science writers, fiction and non-fiction writers, a graphic memoirist, translators, filmmakers, composers, musicians, choreographers, and a linguist. They came from Denmark, Saudi Arabia, Palestine, Kazakhstan, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Japan. Of the U.S. residents, there was a heavy representation from Brooklyn and L.A. They were humble despite Pulitzers, Guggenheims, National Book Awards, NAACP Image Awards, gallery showings, Netflix shows, and a MacArthur. Each of us felt lucky to be there. My days went like this. posts.title: Something Old, Something New
posts.description: What’s something new you’re starting or trying? A new workout, a new habit, a new club, a new relationship? Tell me about it in the comments. A new novel has been calling me—a sequel to Up from the Blue . I’d been toying with the idea for a few years because the characters aren’t done with me. But a few weeks ago, I was taking a walk, and an idea I’ve been obsessed with all my life collided with something current I’ve been struggling with. And I realized the story is made for Tillie. Once I let myself imagine it, scenes rushed in, as did old characters… and new ones. I’m excited to see where it all takes me. I’m learning to love this process again—no time table, no idea why an image or a setting or phrase won’t let me go. I’ve learned to follow seeming tangents, not sure if or how they’re related. posts.title: The Finish Line
posts.description: Tell me about something you recently finished. It can be a race, a book, a project, a course, a sleeve of Oreos, anything at all. This is a picture of the finished book. Working title: Shearwater . I spent years inside this abandoned hospital, both literally and figuratively. Spent hours talking with former nurses, doctors, ward attendants, patients, foster parents, a locksmith, a night watchman, a maintenance worker, urban explorers, and the folks who shared original records and keys with me. The result landed somewhere I didn’t expect: a story about motherhood and chosen family. Six years of research and writing. That may sound long to you, but I’m always struck by the near impossibility of going from that first kernel of an idea to a blank page. Working and working at something that feels intangible, over your head, and never sure if you’ll pull it off. There are all kinds of next steps after you finish a book.
